content:
The numbering of axioms in the definition of class SetTheory at Lines 80-110 of Section_3_1.lean does not correspond to that of the text. There are good reasons for this, since the the text and the Lean translation develop set theory differently, but I do not see any comment to alert the reader not to look for a precise correspondence. In fact, this paragraph (Lines 8-10) would appear to suggest that there should be such a correspondence:

as faithful as possible to the original text of Analysis I, Section 3.1. All numbering refers to
the original text.

Am I missing something?

I'm enjoying this route to learning Lean enormously, but I'm new to Zulip, so please let me know if this is not the sort of comment that belongs here.

Can you be more specific about the issue? The axioms in Lean (as well as the supporting operations needed to state those axioms) are linked to their Analysis I counterparts via a comment at the end of the relevant lines).

Thanks for that prompt reply. It's possible that I have an outdated edition of Analysis I (on Kindle). Refering to that edition:
Axiom 3.1 is the same in Lean and in Analysis I.
Axiom3.2 in Lean is extensionality, which doesn't exist in the text, as equality of sets is defined by extension. Instead, Axiom3.2 in the text is Empty Set.
Axiom 3.3 in Lean is Empty Set, whereas Axiom 3.3 in the text is essentially the Pair Axiom.
Axiom 3.4 in Lean is Singleton, which will generate a Pair axiom in conjunction with the next axiom.
Axiom 3.5 in Lean is Union (of pairs of sets), whereas Axiom 3.5 in the text is Specification.
. . .
Needless to say, there are necessarily subsequent discrepancies. I wouldn't change anything, but a comment up front might save some readers (like me) some confusion. Btw, I've followed you for years and I am very grateful for all you do for the mathematical community.

Ah, that is likely from the third edition or earlier. From the fourth edition onwards, extensionality is an axiom (it was pointed out that it isn't well-defined as a definition, and indeed Lean would not have been able to formalize it as such).
Thanks for the clarification. I have the third edition in Kindle, purchased about a month ago. Amazon should have mentioned that it is not up-to-date.
